name: Emeka Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the billing line for an energy supplier, in a contact centre on the edge of town, in what used to be a carpet mill. I log on at eight, take about seventy calls a day, mostly people whose bills went up or whose prepay meter ran dry. I like the ones where I can actually sort something, like getting an old lady's direct debit lowered before winter. What wears me out is the angry ones at four o'clock, and the screen timing every second I'm not talking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the screen timing look like, and who's watching it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's a little clock for after-call work, and if I go over ninety seconds it turns amber, then red. Gary, my team leader, gets a list every morning, and he's alright, but he has to chase it because his boss chases him. They put a box on the side of the screen last year that suggests what to type to customers. I switched it off the first week and I've never turned it back on, because it reads like a robot wrote it, which I suppose it did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Half the people in our break room were sure the chat bot would take all of us by Christmas, and here we are still answering phones. Online I'd probably share some article about AI being overhyped and laugh about it with my mates from school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't fix anything for me, because my problems were never AI. I'm on low pay, Ruth and I rent a two-bed above a takeaway on Canal Street, and we have maybe three weeks of money if one of us stops working. A flat world just means the same squeeze, same rent rise every spring, same overtime I need to make it to payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep picking up Saturday overtime, because that's the only way we've ever caught up. I'd finally go to a union meeting instead of just paying the subs, because the pay rise this year was below what our rent went up. And I'd keep that suggestion box switched off, plateau or no plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then tired. Getting through it is like dodging a car and then remembering you still can't pay the gas bill. I'm not scared of the robot in this one, I'm scared of the same slow grind going on forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine bits still get automated a little. What would that touch in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said the routine bits still get automated a little. What would that touch in your day?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the money stays this tight even with nothing changing, what would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the after-call notes and the payment plans, the easy stuff where I'd get a breather between hard calls. If the computer does the easy calls, I get the angry ones back to back all day. Precious, who I eat lunch with, says that's already happening on the chat team, and she comes out of her shift white as a sheet.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was overblown and our phones are still ringing.
I'd joke online with **school mates** that the robots never turned up.
think: My real problem is **low pay** and rent, not AI.
With about **three weeks** of savings, a flat world still means a constant squeeze.
do: Keep working Saturday **overtime** to cover the yearly rent rise.
Go to a **union meeting** instead of only paying the subs.
feel: Brief **relief**, then tiredness at the same **slow grind** going on.
S0.quote: Getting through it is like dodging a car and then remembering you still can't pay the gas bill.
fieldNote: Even with no AI shock, **thin savings** and below-inflation pay keep him on edge.
He fears automation would leave him only the **angry calls**, back to back.
His resistance is **personal**: he switched off the suggestion tool in week one.

steps.text: Keep taking Saturday overtime shifts to cover the spring rent rise
Go to the next union branch meeting about the pay offer
Cancel the unused gym membership and drop to a cheaper phone plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the company should be made to keep people on, not just cut and call it progress. Online I'd be the one sharing the union's posts and arguing in the comments. I'd say customers hate bots, which is true, because I hear it twenty times a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm the exact person this card is about. Answering customers is right there in the list, and I'm average at the job, not the best, so when they cut the floor from three hundred to a hundred and fifty, I'm not in the half that stays. There's one other call centre within an hour on the bus, and they'd be doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get properly active in the union, go to meetings and push for a no-redundancy deal before the bots come in. I'd tell Ruth we need to stop the holiday fund and put every spare bit into savings, even if it's forty a month. I'd look at the care agency she works for, because that's hands-on and they're always short, though the pay's even worse than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. My granddad was told the carpet mill was closing in this same building, and I'd be the second one in my family to get that news here. I'd be angry too, mostly at the owners, who'll pay themselves more for doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the AI tools. If the company said learn them or leave, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You've never used the AI tools. If the company said learn them or leave, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably drag my feet and do the bare minimum training, if I'm honest. I know that's not clever. But I don't believe learning to babysit the thing that replaces me is a real career, and I'd rather spend my energy fighting for a proper deal.

say: I'd say the company must **keep people on**, not cut jobs and call it progress.
I'd share **union posts** online and say customers hate talking to bots.
think: Answering customers is **first in line**, and as an average agent I'd be cut.
There's only **one other call centre** within an hour by bus.
do: Push the union for a **no-redundancy deal** before the bots arrive.
Stop the holiday fund and **save** every spare bit, even forty a month.
Ask about **care work** at his partner's agency, despite worse pay.
feel: Sick, like his granddad when the **carpet mill** closed.
**Angry** at owners who'd pay themselves more for cutting staff.
S1.quote: My granddad was told the carpet mill was closing in this same building, and I'd be the second one in my family to get that news here.
fieldNote: He openly admits he'd **drag his feet** on AI training, choosing to fight instead.
His family history at the **mill** shapes how he reads job cuts.
He worries about colleagues on **chat** and the older agents more than himself out loud.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a no-redundancy agreement before the chatbot rollout
Stop the holiday fund and save forty a month instead
Ask Ruth's care agency about hands-on support worker shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest robbery in history, and I'd mean it. At work I'd be telling everyone to join the union that week, not next month. Online I'd be calling for the government to tax these companies and pay people while they sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished in this job within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. It's all thinking work, phones and screens, so there's no three years of grace for me like a plumber gets. I've got three weeks of money and no degree, and I've no idea what job is left for someone like me in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd tell Ruth and we'd sit down with the bills and cut everything that isn't rent, food and heating. I'd sign every petition and go to every march, because that's the only lever I've got. Once it lands, I'd go straight to the care agency or a warehouse, anything with hands, and I'd apply for whatever support the government puts out, the first day it opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like falling down stairs in the dark. I don't have a plan, and two years isn't enough to make one when you're living payday to payday. I'd be frightened, and I'd be furious, and I don't know which would win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ruth's in care work, which is hands-on. Does that change things for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's in care work, which is hands-on. Does that change things for your household?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother, asking to move back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. My partner Ruth's care job lasts till the robots come, but her wage alone won't cover our rent. That's 2031 on this card, so for three years we'd be living on what she earns, which is about what I earn now. We'd probably have to move in with my mother in her two-bed, which none of us would enjoy.

say: I'd call it the **biggest robbery** in history.
I'd urge everyone to **join the union** and demand the government tax AI firms.
think: His job is all thinking work, so he expects to be **finished** within a year.
With **no degree** and three weeks saved, he can't see what job remains.
do: Cut every bill except **rent, food and heating** this month.
Join every **march and petition** for support.
Apply for **care or warehouse** work and government help the day it opens.
feel: Like **falling down stairs** in the dark, with no plan.
S2.quote: My partner Ruth's care job lasts till the robots come, but her wage alone won't cover our rent.
fieldNote: He grasps the **three-year gap**: his partner's hands-on job outlasts his own.
He has **no plan** beyond protest and moving in with his mother.
Going back home at 27 would feel like **going backwards** ten years.

steps.text: Cut every bill except rent, food and heating straight away
March with the union for an AI tax and wage support
Move with Ruth into his mother's two-bed flat
Apply for government support the first day it opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make them share it, so let's use them. At work I'd be pushing hard for the union to get a deal on retraining money and notice periods. Online I'd say the same thing, louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't save my job at the call centre, it just tells me the date. I'd still be out by 2031, but at least I'd see it coming. The part that worries me is I know myself, and I'd probably still be sitting at the same desk in year four, hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself do one thing a year, that's the deal I'd make with Ruth. Year one, get on the union's committee and get the redundancy terms written down. Year two, start a care certificate at the college in the evenings, because care is hands-on and buys me till about 2034. And we'd try to put fifty a month away, even if it means no takeaways from downstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but less like falling. More like knowing the rent's going up in spring, you can't stop it, you just have to get ready. I'd still be angry about who gets rich off it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably still be at the same desk in year four. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd probably still be at the same desk in year four. Why?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Care work pays less than you earn now. How would you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because changing is hard for me, and the job's familiar, and every month there's a reason to wait. I didn't even switch on the suggestion box. Ruth says I'd stay on a sinking ship if it had a decent canteen, and she's not wrong.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to make companies share the gains.
I'd push the union for **retraining money** and longer notice periods.
think: Five years doesn't save his job; it just tells him **the date**.
He fears he'd still be **at the same desk** in year four, hoping.
do: Join the **union committee** and get redundancy terms written down.
Start an evening **care certificate** in year two.
Save **fifty a month**, giving up takeaways.
feel: Heavy but steadier, like a **rent rise** you can see coming.
Still **angry** at who gets rich from it.
S3.quote: Five years doesn't save my job at the call centre, it just tells me the date.
fieldNote: He knows his own **inertia** and sets himself one task a year to beat it.
He sees care work as a **poor trade**: less pay for three more years.
Union work remains his first and **most natural** response.

steps.text: Join the union branch committee and get redundancy terms agreed
Enrol in an evening care certificate at the local college
Save fifty a month by dropping takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone to be thrown out. At work I'd be saying the union should negotiate a ten-year plan, starting now. Online, same as always, tax them and share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and I'd have to be doing something else by then. Ten years makes me feel less trapped, but it also makes it easy to put off, and putting things off is my worst habit. I'd still expect to lose this job, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the phones for now, because the money's steady and Ruth and I need it. I'd do the care qualification slowly, a module a year, and maybe look at training as a support worker for adults with learning disabilities, which I think robots would struggle with longest. And I'd stay on at the union, because a decade of pressure could actually win something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick, more of a dull worry. Like knowing your boiler's old: it'll go one day, you just hope you've saved for it. I'd still lie awake on bad weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now, who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where I'm with people in a room, not on a headset. I liked looking after my granddad when he was ill, I was good at it. Maybe running a small team of support workers, if I've learned enough by then.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for throwing anyone out.
I'd ask the union for a **ten-year plan** and tax on the big firms.
think: He still expects to **lose this job**, just later, at thirty-seven.
The long warning makes it easy to **put off**, his worst habit.
do: Stay on the phones for the **steady wage** for now.
Take the **care qualification** one module a year.
Keep up **union work** to win a fair deal.
feel: A **dull worry**, like an old boiler waiting to go.
S4.quote: Ten years makes me feel less trapped, but it also makes it easy to put off, and putting things off is my worst habit.
fieldNote: He sees **support work** with people as his most robot-proof path.
He blames **owners and government**, not the engineers.
He admits he might **blame himself** if he wastes the decade.

steps.text: Keep working billing-line shifts for the steady wage
Complete one care qualification module each year at college
Stay active in the union pushing for a ten-year transition deal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile, because I'd have nothing to stand on. What would help is money while people retrain, paid properly, not a form you fill in for six weeks. And a union deal so they can't just switch the floor off on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. A lot of the people I talk to are old, or broke, or can't read their bill, and a bot won't explain why their meter cut off. That bothers me as much as my own job.

headlineQuote: A lot of the people I talk to are old, or broke, or can't read their bill, and a bot won't explain why their meter cut off.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old** billing-line agent at an energy supplier, renting a flat with his partner Ruth.
He has about **three weeks** of savings and low pay, so even a quiet AI future feels like a grind.
He is a **union** man by instinct who switched off the AI tool and won't learn it willingly.
Across the scenarios he moves from **anxious** to panicked, with care work as his only real fallback.
He worries as much about **vulnerable customers** losing a human voice as about his own job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no savings and no plan to stand on.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid **retraining money** without weeks of forms.
A **union deal** stopping sudden mass layoffs.
